title: Boulders where they don't belong
teaches: How glaciers grow, flow, carry rock and drop it, and how Agassiz argued for an ice age

blocks.text: In the woods above the town of Neuchâtel, in western Switzerland, sits a granite boulder the size of a small house, known as the Pierre à Bot. The Jura mountains it rests on are made of limestone, laid down in layers like those in lesson 3, with no granite anywhere in the range. The nearest granite of the boulder's exact kind crops out around the Mont Blanc massif in the high Alps of the Valais, more than 100 kilometres away across Lake Neuchâtel and the Swiss plateau.

blocks.caption: An erratic boulder beside a path at Sainte-Croix, in the Swiss Jura.
Western Switzerland: the Valais, the long valley of the Rhône in the Alps, and across the plateau, the Jura. Granite boulders from the Valais lie on the Jura's slopes above Neuchâtel.

options.title: From the Alps to the Jura
options.alt: A shaded relief map of western Switzerland: the high Alps in the southeast cut by the deep valley of the Rhône running west past Brig and Sion to Lake Geneva; the Swiss plateau with Lake Neuchâtel; and the long ridges of the Jura in the northwest.

blocks.text: Millions of these stranded blocks, or **erratics**, lie scattered across northern Europe and North America: Scandinavian granite on the plains of northern Germany, Canadian bedrock across New England and the Midwest, boulders from British Columbia all over the Puget Lowland. The surrounding sheet of loose sand, clay and stones was long known as **drift**, from the belief that it had drifted into place during Noah's flood, or, as Charles Lyell later proposed, dropped from melting icebergs on a sea that once submerged the land. Neither explanation could account for all the evidence on the ground.

blocks.caption: Yeager Rock on the Waterville Plateau in Washington, a boulder left by the Okanogan lobe of the ice sheet. The car gives the scale.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Erratics are boulders resting far from the bedrock they came from.
The Pierre à Bot is Alpine granite sitting on Jura limestone, more than 100 km from its source.

blocks.text: People who lived beside the glaciers had worked out a simpler explanation. In 1815 Jean-Pierre Perraudin, a chamois hunter from the Val de Bagnes in the Valais, pointed out to visiting naturalists that the scarred rock and stray boulders far down his valley looked just like the ground newly uncovered by the glacier high above, and argued that the ice had once reached all the way down there. The cantonal engineer Ignace Venetz took him seriously and convinced his friend Jean de Charpentier, a mine director at Bex; by the 1830s Charpentier was making the case that ice from the Alps had once filled the entire Rhône valley and spread across the plateau to the Jura.

Louis Agassiz, a young professor at Neuchâtel already known for his work on fossil fish, visited Charpentier in the summer of 1836 expecting to talk him out of his mistake. After a tour of the Valais he came back a convert, and characteristically carried the idea much further. In July 1837, in his presidential address to the Swiss Society of Natural Sciences at Neuchâtel, he proposed that a great sheet of ice had once covered Europe from the North Pole to the Mediterranean before the Alps themselves were pushed up. Even Charpentier thought this speculative sweep went beyond the evidence, and most of the audience was appalled, yet Agassiz threw himself into fieldwork in the Alps, camping on the Unteraar glacier for several summers to measure its flow and publishing his *Études sur les glaciers* in 1840.

blocks.caption: Louis Agassiz, photographed in later life.

blocks.text: The bedrock beneath the boulders carried its own record. A moving glacier holds stones frozen into its sole and drags them under great weight across the rock floor, cutting parallel scratches called **striations** and grinding the surface to a dull polish. Below the snouts of living Alpine glaciers, that same scratched and polished rock could be followed step by step down the valleys and out onto the limestone of the Jura. Across the valley floors curved long ridges of unlayered clay, sand and angular stones, **moraines** dumped where the ice margin had once stood, identical in shape and makeup to the ridges still banking up at the ends of active glaciers.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Alpine glaciers leave erratics, scratched and polished bedrock, and moraines; the same features far beyond today's ice show where it once reached.
Agassiz argued in 1837 for an ice age that had covered much of Europe.

blocks.text: A glacier begins as snow that survives the summer. High in the mountains, winter snowfall exceeds summer melting, so each year's snow is buried under the next, compressing first into a dense granular pack called **firn** and eventually, as the air between the grains is squeezed out, into solid blue ice. Lower down the valley the air is warmer, and summer melting strips away more ice than winter snow replaces. The boundary between the upper zone of net gain and the lower zone of net loss is the **equilibrium line**, which lies near the snowline at the end of summer.

Although ice is a crystalline solid, under the weight of tens of metres of overlying snow and ice it deforms internally and creeps downhill like very stiff pitch, while also sliding over a wet bed. A line of stakes that Agassiz drove across the Unteraar glacier in 1841 had bowed downvalley by as much as 75 metres when he returned the following summer. This flow continuously transfers ice from the accumulation zone above the equilibrium line to the melting zone below it, and the glacier's snout settles at the point where the total yearly melt below the line matches the total yearly gain above it. If the climate cools or winter snowfall increases, the equilibrium line shifts lower down the mountain, putting more area into the gain zone; the glacier then creeps farther down the valley until the extra surface exposed to warmer air at its lower end restores the balance. When the climate warms, melting outpaces supply and the snout melts back.

While the snout may stay in one place or even retreat up the valley, the ice within the glacier only ever moves downhill, carrying rock with it. Frost-shattered blocks that tumble onto the ice from the cliffs above, along with stones plucked from the bedrock underneath, travel down the valley inside the moving ice regardless of their weight and melt out at the snout. Whenever the climate holds steady long enough for the snout to linger at one spot, the steady delivery of debris piles up an end moraine; when the ice finally melts back, the moraine ridge and the largest boulders remain stranded on the valley floor.

blocks.caption: The Aletsch Glacier in Switzerland. The dark stripes running along the ice are moraines, bands of rock carried downhill by the glacier.

The path of the Rhône glacier from its source to the Jura, in long section (heights exaggerated). The red dashed line is the equilibrium line; the brown ridge is the moraine at the farthest point the ice has reached. A simplified model of the glacier, not a forecast.
blocks.task: Change the climate until the glacier reaches the Jura

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Above the equilibrium line snow accumulates; below it, ice melts away.
A glacier flows from where it gains to where it loses ice, and its length adjusts until the two balance.
Glaciers carry rock of any size and drop it where the ice melts, building moraines at their ends.

parts.title: The Rhône glacier at its greatest

blocks.text: Today the Rhône glacier is about 8 kilometres long and shrinking rapidly; each summer, workers drape white insulating fleece over the tip of its tongue to slow the melting around a tourist ice grotto. At the peak of the last glaciation, between about 24,000 and 20,000 years ago, that same river of ice filled the Valais to a depth of well over a kilometre above Martigny, spilled out through the Lake Geneva basin, and fanned across the Swiss plateau until it banked against the eastern slope of the Jura, some 200 kilometres from its source. A lobe of ice even split off to the northeast toward Solothurn, while the Pierre à Bot, fallen from the cliffs of the Mont Blanc massif, rode the left flank of the glacier across the plateau and was left high on the limestone hillside above Neuchâtel as the ice wasted away.

In the model above, keeping snowfall at today's rate and cooling the air by roughly 10 °C is enough to drive the ice all the way to the Jura. Independent reconstructions from ice-age pollen and old moraines in the Alps agree well with that figure, placing the equilibrium line 1,000 to 1,500 metres lower than today at the height of the glaciation. Increasing snowfall lowers the equilibrium line in the same way a temperature drop does, because deeper winter snow takes longer to melt in summer. A small drop in the equilibrium line produces a huge advance for two reasons: mountain valleys broaden downward, so a lower line brings a much larger area of the drainage basin into the snow-gathering zone, and as the growing glacier thickens, its own upper surface rises into colder air, helping it gather snow faster still.

Agassiz was right that great sheets of ice had overrun the northern continents, though the history of the ice proved far more intricate than a single grand freeze. Over the past 2.6 million years the ice has advanced and retreated dozens of times, and at the height of the last advance a continental ice sheet up to 3 kilometres thick buried Canada and reached south to the Ohio and Missouri rivers and across the Puget Lowland. Why the ice sheets grow and waste away on such a regular timetable is the subject of the next lesson.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: About 20,000 years ago the Rhône glacier reached the Jura, 200 km from its source, carrying the erratics there.
The equilibrium line in the Alps was then about 1,000 to 1,500 m lower than today.
Multiple advances and retreats of the ice have occurred over the last 2.6 million years.

blocks.caption: Five questions on glaciers and erratics
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why does the Pierre à Bot point to transport by glacier ice rather than by a raging flood?
choices: It is an angular house-sized block of Alpine granite perched high on a Jura limestone slope, alongside striated bedrock and moraines, where flowing water could neither lift it nor sort it
It is made of the same limestone as the Jura ridge it rests on, showing it was carved in place
Its surface is vitrified and melted from the friction of sliding down the Alps
items.why: Even a catastrophic flood loses speed when it spreads out of a mountain valley, and cannot carry a house-sized block 100 km across a basin and halfway up a mountain range. Moving ice carries blocks of any weight without sorting them by size.

items.ask: What defines the equilibrium line on a glacier?
choices: The elevation where the year's snowfall exactly matches the year's melting
The boundary at the base of the glacier where solid ice begins to slide over wet bedrock
The line along the valley floor where the glacier snout deposits its terminal moraine
items.why: Above the equilibrium line, snow accumulates from year to year; below it, summer melting removes more ice than winter snow adds.

items.ask: If the climate cools and the equilibrium line drops by 500 metres, how does the glacier reach a new steady length?
choices: It advances down the valley until the extra melting across its newly expanded lower tongue matches the extra snow gathered above the lowered line
It retreats up the valley, because cooler summers reduce the meltwater lubricating its bed
It thickens in place without changing length, because ice stops flowing at lower temperatures
items.why: Lowering the equilibrium line increases the area gaining snow and shrinks the area losing ice; the glacier must extend farther into warmer, lower elevations before yearly loss once again equals yearly gain.

items.ask: How do striations form on bedrock?
choices: Stones frozen into the base of a moving glacier are dragged under high pressure across the rock floor, cutting parallel grooves
Meltwater streams rushing beneath the ice carve narrow, winding channels into the stone
Repeated freezing and thawing of rainwater splits the surface of the rock along parallel mineral grains
items.why: Ice by itself is softer than most rock, so it is the rock fragments held like teeth in the sole of the glacier that gouge and polish the bed as the ice slides overhead.

items.ask: If you find a curved ridge of unsorted clay, sand, and angular boulders stretching across a dry mountain valley, what does it record?
choices: A line where a glacier's snout held steady for years while internal ice flow kept delivering rock debris to the melting edge
The point high in the mountains where snow first compacted into glacier ice
The speed at which the glacier retreated when the climate warmed
items.why: Even when a glacier's snout stays at the same place on the map, ice inside the glacier continues to flow downhill to the snout and melt there, piling up all its carried debris into a terminal moraine.

summary: **Ice leaves signs far beyond today’s glaciers.** Erratic boulders, scratched rock and moraines show where it once reached.
**A glacier is a balance of snow and melt.** It gains above its equilibrium line, loses below, and flows from one zone to the other.
**A glacier’s length adjusts until gain equals loss.**
**Cooling makes glaciers advance.** A colder climate lowers the equilibrium line.
**There was an ice age.** About 20,000 years ago the Rhône glacier crossed the Swiss plateau and left Alpine boulders on the Jura.
